p: A Chinese menu has hundreds of possible dishes. Chinese signs do not. The same fifty or so words turn up on every metro platform, shop door and toilet corridor from Beijing to Kunming, and most of them are two characters long.

That makes signs the easiest Chinese you will ever read. Learn to recognise 出口 (exit), 禁止 (forbidden) and 洗手间 (toilet) by shape and you are already reading a large share of what is on the walls. Mainland China uses simplified characters, which is what these tables show. Hong Kong, Macau and Taiwan use traditional characters, so 出口 looks the same but 电梯 becomes 電梯 and 厕所 becomes 廁所. Tova reads both.
The first group is the one that gets you out of a building. 口 means mouth, and on a sign it means an opening — a way in or out.

p: Large Chinese metro stations can have a dozen exits spread over several streets. Coming up the wrong one can cost you ten minutes and a road crossing.
ol: **Look up the exit before you arrive.** Map apps and hotel directions usually name an exit letter — "Exit D" or "D口". Write it down.
**Follow 出口 first, then the letter.** On the platform, overhead boards show 出口 with an arrow. Nearer the gates the boards split by letter.

**Read the landmark list under each letter.** Exit boards list the streets, malls and buildings above that exit. This is where the camera earns its place: capture the board and you get every landmark in English with its pinyin, which you can match against the name your hotel sent you.
**Check for 无障碍 if you have luggage.** Not every exit has a lift or escalator. The accessible ones are marked, usually with the wheelchair symbol as well.

sections.h2: A sign you do not understand on a door
p: You reach a door with red characters and no English. Before you push it, look for 禁止 or 请勿 at the start. If either is there, whatever comes next is not allowed.

禁止入内 and 闲人免进 both mean you should not go through. 禁止吸烟 in a stairwell means the stairwell is not the smoking area, however many cigarette ends are on the floor. If the sign is longer than four or five characters, capture it: long signs are often rules or opening hours, and the detail matters.
Shop doors work the same way. 营业时间 followed by numbers is the opening hours, written on a 24-hour clock. 休息 on its own, often hung on a card, means closed for now.

ul: **Reading 出 and 入 the wrong way round.** 出 (chū) is out, 入 (rù) is in. 入 is easy to confuse with 人 (person) — the strokes lean the other way.
**Assuming 酒店 is a bar.** It is a hotel. A bar is usually 酒吧 (jiǔbā).
**Reading a discount as a percentage off.** 七折 means you pay 70% of the price, not that 70% is taken off.
**Trusting the English on the sign.** Many signs carry an English line, and some are machine-translated nonsense. The characters are the reliable part.

**Waiting for a live read on a stylised sign.** Calligraphy, neon and very old shopfronts are hard for any camera. Get closer, tap the shutter for a still capture, and accept that a heavily decorative sign may still come back wrong.

sections.h2: Why your translation app stops working when you land
p: Mainland China filters international internet traffic, and Google's services are on the wrong side of that filter. Google Translate — the app most travellers already have — cannot reach its servers from a Chinese network. Google ran a China-specific version at translate.google.cn for years, but **shut it down in October 2022**, so the old workaround is gone too.

What makes this worse than a normal outage is how it fails. The app opens. The camera turns on. You point it at a menu and nothing happens, or the text freezes half-translated. There is no error telling you the country you are standing in is the problem, so most people assume their phone is broken or the hotel Wi-Fi is slow, and keep retrying at the exact moment they needed an answer.

The fix is not a single app. It is deciding, before you fly, which of your tools work **on the device itself** — with the aeroplane in flight mode, no SIM, no Wi-Fi — because that is the only capability the filter cannot touch. We ran the main apps through exactly that test in [our comparison of the best translator apps for China](/translate/best-translator-app-for-china/).
Tested on an iPhone on a mainland Chinese network in September 2026. Treat it as a starting point rather than gospel: what is reachable changes, sometimes within a single week.

sections.callout: The row that catches people out is Google Translate's. Its **offline packs keep working** even though the app cannot reach the network — but only if you downloaded them before you arrived. Downloading them from inside China is exactly the thing that will not work.

sections.h2: Set it up before you fly
p: Do all of this on your home Wi-Fi. Every step needs a connection that mainland China will not give you. If you are not sure what to download, [the offline translator checklist](/translate/offline-translator-china/) explains the three kinds of offline pack and which ones you need.
ol: **Download offline language packs in every translation app you plan to use.** In Tova, Settings → Offline packs. In Apple Translate, Settings → Translate → Downloaded Languages. In Google Translate, the download arrow next to Chinese.

**Test each one in flight mode before you leave the house.** Turn on aeroplane mode, then actually translate something. An app that shows a spinner in your kitchen will show the same spinner in Chengdu.
**Photograph the things you will need offline** — your hotel booking with the Chinese address, your visa page, the Chinese name of anywhere you plan to go. A screenshot survives a dead network.
**Write down your hotel address in Chinese characters** and keep it on paper. Every taxi conversation starts there, and paper does not run out of battery.
**Install anything you might want later, now.** The App Store itself is reachable in China, but downloads can be slow and some apps are unavailable in the Chinese storefront.

sections.h2: Roaming and eSIMs: the workaround business travellers use
p: If you keep your home SIM active and pay for international roaming, your data is usually routed back through your home carrier's network before it reaches the internet. In practice that means you are browsing as if you were still at home, and the services blocked on local networks often load normally.

The same is true of most travel eSIMs sold for China, which is why they are popular with business travellers. It is not a guarantee — some route locally, and carriers change their arrangements — so check with your provider rather than assuming, and never make roaming your only plan. Roaming data is also expensive enough that camera translation of a long menu is a real cost.
A local Chinese SIM is the opposite: cheap, fast, and filtered exactly like every other domestic connection.

sections.h2: If you are already in China with nothing downloaded
p: Not ideal, but not hopeless.
ul: **Apple Translate is already on your iPhone** and is reachable. It will not give you pinyin, but it will give you meaning.
**The App Store works.** You can still install an app that translates on-device — you just cannot install one that needs Google.
**Hotel Wi-Fi is filtered too.** It is the same internet. A VPN you install after arriving is also likely to be blocked; they have to be set up beforehand.
**Ask.** Staff at any hotel above budget level generally read some English, and pointing at a phone screen works better than you would expect.

sections.h2: Why pinyin matters more than you think
p: Most translation apps give you the meaning and stop. That is enough to order lunch, and not enough to say the name of the dish, ask where the bathroom is, or read the same character again tomorrow and recognise it.

Pinyin — the romanisation above each character — turns a translation into something you can pronounce out loud. In a country where the gap between reading and speaking is the whole problem, that is the difference between pointing at a phone and having a conversation. Tova prints it above every character; Pleco gives it in dictionary lookups; the mainstream translators mostly do not.

The same gap shows up where you least expect it. Chinese stations are named city + direction + 站, so Hangzhou, Hangzhou East and Hangzhou South are three different places and the difference is one character — see [which Chinese train station is on your ticket](/translate/chinese-train-stations/).

sections.h2: Cantonese is not Mandarin with an accent
p: Cantonese is the everyday language of Hong Kong, Macau and much of Guangdong, including Guangzhou. It shares most of its characters with Mandarin, but the sounds are different enough that a Mandarin speaker and a Cantonese speaker cannot follow each other in conversation.

That is the problem with using Hanyu Pinyin in Hong Kong. Pinyin is built for Mandarin. Put pinyin above a Cantonese menu and you get the Mandarin reading of every character, which is not what anyone in the restaurant will say. 飲茶, the word for going out for dim sum, is yǐn chá in Mandarin and jam2 caa4 in Cantonese. Say the first in a Hong Kong teahouse and you will be understood only because the staff guess.

Jyutping is the romanisation the Linguistic Society of Hong Kong designed for Cantonese. It is what Tova uses when you set the language to Cantonese, and it is what the [free Jyutping converter](/tools/jyutping-converter/) on this site produces from any text you paste.
Jyutping marks tone with a number after each syllable rather than an accent over a vowel. Cantonese has six tones, and changing the tone changes the word. The classic set uses the syllable si:
The same characters read in Mandarin pinyin and in Jyutping. None of these are close enough to swap.

ol: **Find the order sheet.** Most dim sum restaurants give you a printed sheet listing every dish, with a box to write the quantity. It is almost entirely characters.

**Capture the whole sheet.** Tap the shutter once and Tova reads the full sheet, with Jyutping above each dish name and the English underneath. For the broader menu vocabulary — cooking methods, proteins, warning words — see [how to read a Chinese menu](/translate/chinese-menu/).
**Mark the boxes, hand it over.** You do not have to say anything. When a trolley or server comes past, 呢個 (ni1 go3, this one) and a point is enough.
**Ask for the bill with 唔該埋單.** m4 goi1 maai4 daan1. A raised hand and a small scribbling gesture works too.

p: Minibuses do not stop at every stop unless someone asks. The route and fare are on a card at the front, usually in characters, so capture it before you get on if you are unsure you have the right one.

When your stop is coming, call out 有落 (jau5 lok6) — getting off — or 前面有落 (cin4 min6 jau5 lok6), getting off ahead. This is the one place where saying it matters more than showing it: the driver is watching the road, not your phone. Practise it with the Jyutping first and tap Listen to hear it.

ul: **Using pinyin in Hong Kong.** It gives you the Mandarin reading. Many people in Hong Kong speak Mandarin, but it is not the language of the street.
**Dropping the tone numbers.** Without them, si could be any of six words. The numbers are the pronunciation, not decoration.
**Mixing up 唔該 and 多謝.** Both mean thank you. 唔該 is for a service — someone holding a door, bringing your food. 多謝 is for a gift or a favour.
**Reading Jyutping as English.** j sounds like English y, so jau5 is close to "yow". c is like ts or ch, so caa4 is close to "chah". eo and oe are vowel sounds with no English equivalent.
**Expecting simplified characters.** Hong Kong and Macau use traditional characters. Guangzhou uses simplified, but the spoken language there is still Cantonese.

p: Chinese has no alphabet, which is why it looks impossible. But reading a sign is not the same as learning the language, and the gap is smaller than it looks.

Characters are not pictures to memorise one by one. Most are built from a **radical** — a component that hints at meaning — plus a component that hints at sound. 河 (river), 湖 (lake) and 海 (sea) all carry the same three-stroke water radical on the left. Once you see it, you see it everywhere.
You are not trying to read fluently. You are trying to recognise enough to know whether the door says entrance or exit, and to say the name of the place you are going.

sections.h2: Tones are not optional, and pinyin shows them
p: Pinyin is the romanisation that turns 你好 into nǐ hǎo. The marks over the vowels are tones, and they change the word rather than decorating it: mā is mother, mǎ is horse, mà is to scold.

Travellers routinely decide tones are a refinement to worry about later. They are not — they are part of the word, in the way that swapping a vowel would be in English. Getting them approximately right is what makes the difference between being understood and being smiled at.
You will get them wrong. Say it anyway; people correct you, and the correction is how you learn.

It matters for your camera settings — a scanner set to the wrong one is slower and less accurate — and it matters almost not at all for speaking. If you are travelling to both, set your app to match where you are standing.
Point-and-read closes the loop the dictionary cannot: you do not need to know a character's pronunciation to look it up, because the camera recognises the shape for you.

Handwriting and calligraphy are still hard, for cameras as much as for learners. Faded signs, brush strokes and stylised restaurant logos defeat every scanner some of the time.

p: Written Japanese uses three scripts at once, often in the same word. Romaji — Japanese written in the Latin alphabet — is the fourth, and it exists mostly for people who cannot read the other three yet. Knowing which script you are looking at tells you a lot before you know what any of it says.

Hiragana and katakana are syllable alphabets of 46 basic characters each: every character is one sound, and the sound never changes. Kanji are the characters borrowed from Chinese, and each has a meaning and usually several readings. A sentence like 駅で水を買います (eki de mizu o kaimasu, I buy water at the station) switches between kanji and hiragana four times.

sections.h2: The romaji rules that trip people up
p: Signs, maps and rail networks in Japan use Hepburn romaji, the system built for English speakers. It is mostly spelled the way it sounds, with a handful of rules that catch everyone out.

head: Japanese
Romaji
The rule
rows: A long vowel is marked with a line, ō. Signs often drop it and write Tokyo; you may also see Toukyou
おお is also a long o
In katakana the dash ー lengthens the vowel before it
A small っ doubles the next consonant — hold it for a beat
Before ch the doubling is written tch
ん is n. Traditional Hepburn writes m before b, m and p, so you will also see shimbun
An apostrophe separates ん from a following vowel: cause
The particle は is read wa, not ha
The particle へ is read e, not he — to the station
The particle を is read o — water, as the object
し ち つ ふ じ
Hepburn spells these as they sound to English ears

sections.callout: Japanese schools also teach a second system, Kunrei-shiki, which writes the same sounds as si, ti, tu and hu — so 富士 can appear as Huzi instead of Fuji. You will rarely see it on signs, but it explains the odd spelling in older textbooks.

p: This is the part that makes kanji hard, and the reason a simple lookup table cannot give you romaji. Most kanji have a Chinese-derived reading (on'yomi), used mainly in compound words, and a native Japanese reading (kun'yomi), used mainly when the character stands alone or takes a hiragana ending. Some have more than one of each, and place names follow their own rules.
The right reading depends on the word the kanji sits in. The table shows how far apart they get.

ol: **Capture the name.** Set the scan language to Japanese and tap the shutter on the sign, ticket or booking. The panel at the bottom of the camera screen shows the romaji above the characters and the English underneath.
**Tap to hear it.** Listen before you say it. Japanese gives every syllable roughly the same length, so Shinjuku is shin-ju-ku, not SHIN-jook.

sections.h2: Reading a label in a konbini
ol: **Look for katakana first.** Many product names are loanwords. Sound out the katakana and you often recognise the English word underneath — サンドイッチ is sandoitchi, sandwich.
**Then the kanji.** Flavours and ingredients are usually kanji: 鶏 for chicken, 豚 for pork. Scan the label if you need the detail.
**Check the dates.** 賞味期限 (shōmi kigen) is best before; 消費期限 (shōhi kigen) is use by.

ul: **Reading romaji as English.** Vowels are always a, i, u, e, o, as in Spanish or Italian. Sake is sa-ke, not sayk. Karaoke is ka-ra-o-ke.
**Dropping long vowels.** They change the word. おばさん obasan is aunt; おばあさん obāsan is grandmother.
**Ignoring the small っ.** 来て kite means come; 切手 kitte means postage stamp.
**Over-pronouncing u.** In desu and masu the u is usually barely heard: dess, mass.
**Reading は as ha everywhere.** It is ha inside a word and wa as a particle. こんにちは ends in wa.
**Expecting one reading per kanji.** 生 alone has at least five common readings. If a romaji dictionary gives you one reading for a character, it is not the whole story.

faqs.a: Romaji is Japanese written in the Latin alphabet. It tells you how a word sounds without needing to read hiragana, katakana or kanji, so ラーメン becomes rāmen. Tova places romaji above the characters rather than replacing the Japanese, so you learn the script as you read.

faqs.a: Kanji came from Chinese and kept a Chinese-derived reading alongside the native Japanese word for the same idea. Which one is used depends on the word, so 生 is nama in draught beer, sei in student, shō in lifetime and u in born. Place names often have readings of their own.

faqs.a: All three mean 東京. Tōkyō is Hepburn with the long vowels marked, Toukyou spells out the kana, and Tokyo is the everyday English spelling that drops the marks. The long vowels do matter when you say it.

p: A translator tells you what a sign means. h1: Translate Japanese signs and station boards
lede: Station boards, exit signs, shop notices and warning placards are where a trip to Japan actually gets hard. Point Tova at one and it reads back in English with romaji above every character.
steps: Set the scan language to Japanese and point the camera at the sign.
Tap the shutter and read the English meaning, with romaji above each character, in the panel below.
Save the ones you will need again, like your station name or hotel address, to Favourites.

p: Big stations in Tokyo, Osaka and Kyoto have English on the main signs, and first-time visitors are often surprised how far that gets them. The trouble starts one layer down: the paper notice taped to a closed exit, the fare adjustment machine, the shop door that says it is shut today, the bus stop in a small town, the warning on a hiking trail.

Those signs use a small, repetitive vocabulary. The same forty or fifty words cover most of what you will meet, and many of them are two kanji long. Learn to recognise the shapes in the tables below and you can usually tell an exit from an entrance before your phone is out of your pocket.
If the scripts are new to you, [reading Japanese with romaji](/translate/read-japanese-romaji/) covers hiragana, katakana and kanji, and the spelling rules that make romaji look odd.

Romaji
What it means
rows: Boarding area, for trains, buses or taxis
Towards — the direction a train is heading
Fare adjustment machine — pay the difference here

Limited express — often needs an extra ticket

p: Transfers are where most people get lost, because a line can change operator, colour and name at the same station.
ol: **Follow 乗り換え, not 出口.** Transfer signs keep you inside the gates. Following an exit sign by mistake puts you outside, and in some stations that means paying again.
**Match the line colour and letter.** Tokyo Metro and Toei lines each have a colour and a letter, and every station has a number, like G09. Those appear on the signs even where the English does not.
**Read 方面 on the platform.** Each platform names the end of the line or a big stop the train is heading towards. Check it against your map app before you board.
**Check the train type.** A 快速 or 特急 can run straight through your station. If yours is small, a 各駅停車 is the safe choice.

**Scan the notice board if something is wrong.** Delays and suspensions often go up in Japanese first. Tap the shutter on the board, then pinch to zoom into the part you need and translate just that region — it is far more reliable than reading a whole crowded board in one go.
**Choose the exit before you leave the platform.** Large stations have dozens of exits, numbered like A1 and B7 or named by direction, and they can be ten minutes' walk apart above ground.
**Get the exit from your map app.** Most walking directions name a station exit. Look for that number or 東口, 西口 and so on in yellow signs above the platform.
**Check the neighbourhood map by the gates.** It shows which exit leads to which street. Scan it if the landmark names are only in Japanese.
**If you exit wrong, go back through the gates.** In many stations that is quicker than walking round the outside.

p: Convenience stores are easy to use without Japanese, but the staff will ask a few quick questions at the till.
ol: **温めますか** (atatamemasu ka) — do you want it heated? Nod for a bento, shake your head for a sandwich.
**袋はご利用ですか** (fukuro wa goriyō desu ka) — do you need a bag? Bags cost a few yen. はい (hai) for yes, 大丈夫です (daijōbu desu) for no thanks.
**ポイントカード** (pointo kādo) — do you have a points card? いいえ (iie), no, is the answer.
**Check 消費期限 on anything fresh.** Dates are usually written year, month, day.

ul: **Mixing up 入口 and 出口.** Both end in 口, mouth or opening. 入 goes in, 出 goes out. The first kanji is the whole difference.
**Reading 準備中 as open.** A shop with its lights on and a sign saying junbichū is not ready for customers yet.
**Missing 定休日.** Many restaurants close one fixed day a week. The door sign names the day, and it is easy to walk past it and wait.
**Taking a 特急 on a regular ticket.** Limited expresses often need a surcharge ticket. The conductor will ask for it.
**Assuming English means complete.** English signs cover the main route. Closures, detours and temporary notices are frequently Japanese only.
**Pointing the camera at a whole board from across the concourse.** Get closer, or capture it and zoom in. Small text at a distance is where every camera translator, Tova included, gets things wrong.

p: A translation tells you a sign says Shimokitazawa. The romaji tells you how to say it to a station attendant, and it matches the name the train announcer uses. That matters when you are listening for your stop, not reading it.

Tova shows the romaji above each character in a panel at the bottom of the camera screen, with the English underneath, and you can tap to hear it. Kanji readings need a connection, because the same character is read differently in different names. Offline, Tova still translates the sign on your phone, but the romaji may not appear. Save your station and hotel address while you have signal. If Korea is next on the trip, [translating Korean signs](/translate/korean-signs/) works the same way, with Revised Romanization.

faqs.q: How do I translate a Japanese sign with my phone?
faqs.a: Open Tova, set the camera scan language to Japanese, point at the sign and tap the shutter. You get the English meaning and romaji above each character, so you can also say the place name aloud when you ask for directions.

faqs.q: Will it read vertical Japanese text?
faqs.a: Usually. Vertical text is common on shopfronts and older signs. If a vertical column comes out jumbled, capture the photo, zoom into that one column and translate just that region.

faqs.q: Does it work on the small print on station boards?
faqs.a: Zoom in first. After you take the shot you can pinch to magnify the photo and translate only the part you are looking at, which is far more reliable than trying to read a whole crowded board at once.

faqs.q: Do I need a data connection in Japan?
faqs.a: Not for a translation. When Tova cannot reach its servers it falls back to on-device translation, so you still get the English. Romaji for kanji does need a connection, so offline you may see the meaning without the reading.

faqs.q: What is the difference between 出口 and 改札?
faqs.a: 改札, kaisatsu, is the line of ticket gates. 出口, deguchi, is the exit from the station to the street. You pass the 改札 first, then follow signs to the numbered 出口 you want.

faqs.q: What does 準備中 mean on a shop door?
faqs.a: It means the shop is preparing and not open yet, or closed between lunch and dinner. The sign for open is 営業中, eigyōchū.

**Capture the whole note first, then the lines that matter.** Addresses, door codes and check-out times are worth a second, closer capture.
**Check numbers against the original.** A 1 and a 7, or a 0 and a 6, are easy to confuse in handwriting. Read them off the paper, not just off the screen.
**Capture the label before you leave the counter.** If the reading looks wrong you can ask while the pharmacist is still there.
**Match the key words against the table above.** Frequency and timing — three times a day, after meals — are what you need to get right.

**Shooting at an angle.** Tilted handwriting on a board or a menu is harder to read than tilted print. Square up.

**Trusting a confident translation of messy writing.** If the source was hard to read, the translation is a guess. Check the characters Tova recognised against the paper — a wrong character produces a fluent, wrong sentence.

metaDesc: Boardroom mode puts three languages on one phone. Add a third speaker, tap the swap arrow to pass the floor; each turn is transcribed, translated, spoken.
keywords: three way translation, three language translator, multi language conversation app, meeting translator, group translator app, boardroom mode, translate conversation three people
h1: Translate a conversation between three languages
lede: Two-way translation covers a taxi. It falls apart the moment a third language joins the table. Boardroom mode keeps three languages on one phone, and you pass the floor from speaker to speaker with a tap.
steps: Turn on Boardroom mode in Settings (a Pro feature), then open the Speak tab.
Set the two main languages, then tap + 3rd in the chip row and choose the third speaker's language.
Before each person talks, tap the swap arrow until their language is highlighted, then tap the mic.

p: Most translator apps are built for two people: you and a waiter, you and a taxi driver. Put a third language at the table — a supplier who speaks Mandarin, a colleague who speaks Japanese, and you in English — and one of you ends up waiting while the other two talk, or someone is drafted in as an interpreter and stops taking part.

Boardroom mode is Tova's answer. It is part of Tova Pro. One phone sits in the middle of the table, holding three languages, and the person holding the floor is whoever you have selected. Each turn is transcribed with its reading, translated, and can be played aloud with Listen.

It is worth being clear about what it is not. It does not listen to the room and work out who is talking. You tell it, with a tap, every time the speaker changes. That sounds like a chore and in practice becomes a rhythm within a few turns — the same rhythm as passing a microphone.

The Speak tab has a row of language chips across the top. With Boardroom on, the row reads: first language, the swap arrow, second language, and a **+ 3rd** chip. Tap + 3rd and pick the third language; that chip then shows the language name, and the third speaker becomes the active one so they can start straight away.

The swap arrow cycles the floor: first speaker, second speaker, third speaker, back to the first. The highlighted chip is the language Tova is listening for. Speech recognition only works in one language at a time, which is why getting the highlight right matters more than anything else in this mode.

Each time you tap the mic, Tova listens for one utterance and stops when the speaker pauses. Tap it again for the next turn. To drop the third speaker, tap the cross on the Boardroom banner and the conversation goes back to two languages.

sections.h3: A supplier meeting with an agent in the room
ol: **Set the languages before anyone sits down.** For example English, Mandarin, and a third language for a colleague. Do a two-line test so everyone sees what happens on the screen.
**Put the phone flat in the middle, screen up.** People read the translation as well as hear it, and numbers are far easier to check on screen than by ear.
**Make one person responsible for the swap arrow.** Usually whoever called the meeting. Everyone else just talks when the highlight is on their language.
**Keep turns to one or two sentences.** Long turns produce long transcripts where a single misheard number hides in the middle. Short turns are easier to correct.
**Confirm prices, quantities and dates in writing afterwards.** Treat the conversation as the negotiation and an email as the record.

sections.h3: A family dinner across three languages
ol: **Choose the languages people actually speak at home.** If grandparents speak Cantonese rather than Mandarin, pick Cantonese — the transcript comes back with Jyutping, which the [Cantonese guide](/translate/cantonese-jyutping/) explains.
**Let whoever holds the phone run the swap arrow.** Nobody else needs to touch it.
**Use Listen for anyone who does not want to read a screen.** The translation is spoken aloud, which suits older relatives better than small text.

sections.h3: A group tour with a local guide
ol: **Set the guide's language plus the two languages in your group.**
**Ask the guide to pause between points.** The mic stops when the speaker stops, so natural pauses are what split the talk into turns.
**Save the useful answers.** Place names and directions can go to Favourites, which keeps the reading so you can show it later.

sections.h2: What works and what does not

head: Works well
Struggles

Everyone expecting the app to know who is talking
Numbers and names checked on screen

Little background noise, or a phone close to the speaker
A loud restaurant with the phone at the far end of the table

ul: **Forgetting to pass the floor.** If the second speaker talks while the first speaker's language is still highlighted, Tova listens in the wrong language and the transcript comes back as nonsense. Tap the arrow first, every time.
**Expecting automatic speaker detection.** Boardroom mode does not detect who is talking. Someone has to select the speaker.

**Assuming every turn is translated for everyone.** Each turn produces one translation. Do a short test exchange first and check which language each speaker's turns come out in, so the person who most needs to follow is not left out.
**A language the phone cannot listen in.** Speech recognition depends on iOS. If Tova says it cannot listen in a language, adding that language's keyboard in iOS Settings usually fixes it.
**Using it for anything legally binding.** Machine translation is good enough to hold a conversation. It is not a certified interpreter, and a contract needs one.

sections.h2: When a human interpreter is still the right call
p: For a first meeting, a site visit or a dinner, Boardroom mode keeps everyone in the conversation without a fourth person at the table. For a signing, a dispute, a medical appointment or anything where one mistranslated word costs real money, pay for an interpreter.

If you are travelling in mainland China, the rest of your translation set-up matters as much as the meeting itself — the [comparison of translator apps for China](/translate/best-translator-app-for-china/) covers which ones keep working without a VPN.

faqs.q: Can an app translate between three languages at once?
faqs.a: Tova's Boardroom mode holds three languages on one phone. You select who is speaking with the swap arrow, and each turn is transcribed, translated and can be read aloud, so a meeting with English, Mandarin and Japanese speakers can keep going without a human interpreter.

faqs.q: Does it detect who is speaking automatically?
faqs.a: No. You tap the swap arrow to choose the speaker before they talk, and it cycles through the first, second and third language in turn. Speech recognition listens in one language at a time, so the selected speaker has to be the one talking.

faqs.q: Who is three-way translation for?
faqs.a: Mixed-language meetings, family dinners across generations and group travel with a local guide — any situation where two-way translation forces someone at the table to sit out.

faqs.q: Is Boardroom mode free?
faqs.a: Boardroom mode is part of Tova Pro. Camera translation, two-way voice translation and all 118 languages are free.

faqs.q: Does each speaker need their own phone?
faqs.a: No. One phone sits between the speakers. Whoever holds it taps the swap arrow to hand the floor to the next person, and Tova switches recognition to that person's language.

faqs.q: Can I use Cantonese as one of the three languages?
faqs.a: Yes. Cantonese is a separate language in Tova from Mandarin, and Cantonese transcripts come back with Jyutping readings rather than pinyin.

title: Best Translator App for China (2026): Honest Comparison
metaDesc: Google Translate is blocked in mainland China. We tested Apple Translate, Baidu, Pleco, DeepL and Tova: what works offline, what shows pinyin, what it costs.
keywords: best translator app for China, translation app China, Google Translate China, Pleco vs Google Translate, offline translator China, China travel app
h1: The best translator app for China, honestly compared
lede: We make one of the apps on this list. So here is the version that is actually useful: what each one does inside mainland China, where ours is the wrong choice, and what we tested to find out.
steps: Decide whether you need meaning only, or meaning plus pronunciation.
Download offline packs for your shortlist before you fly — none of them can do it once you land.
Test each app in aeroplane mode at home. An app that stalls in your kitchen will stall in Xi'an.

p: **If you want one free app and nothing else: Apple Translate**, if you carry an iPhone. It is already installed, it is not blocked, and it works offline once you download Chinese.
**If you are learning the language: Pleco.** It is a dictionary rather than a translator, it is entirely on-device, and nothing else comes close for looking up a character you half-recognise.

**If you need to read signs and menus fast, with pronunciation: that is what we built Tova for.** It is not the best choice for long documents or for European languages, and we will say so below. If menus are the main worry, start with [how to read a Chinese menu](/translate/chinese-menu/).
sections.callout: Everything here was tested on a mainland Chinese network in **September 2026**. What is reachable from inside China changes without notice, sometimes within a week. Check before you rely on any of it.

sections.h2: What each one does inside China

p: Still the best general-purpose translator in the world, and the wrong tool for this particular country. Google's services are filtered in mainland China and the China-specific version was retired in 2022, so the app opens and then quietly fails to do anything.

The exception is worth knowing: **its offline packs keep working**, because they run on your phone rather than on Google's servers. Download Chinese before you fly and you have a usable — if basic — offline translator. Downloading it after you arrive is the part that will not work.
**Use it if** you already rely on it and remember to prepare. **Skip it if** you are deciding fresh, because you are choosing an app whose main strength is switched off.

The best choice for most travellers with an iPhone, if not the most exciting one. It is not blocked, it is already installed, and its offline mode is genuinely offline once you download a language in Settings.

It is also plainer than the alternatives. Camera translation exists but is less forgiving of bad lighting and handwriting than dedicated scanners, and it does not print readings above individual characters, so it tells you what a sign means without helping you say it.
**Use it if** you want zero setup and zero cost. **Skip it if** you are trying to learn anything as you go.

A Chinese product on Chinese infrastructure, so it is fast and reachable everywhere Google is not. Its Chinese-English translation is good, and it handles Chinese internet slang better than Western tools.
The interface is largely in Chinese, which is an obstacle precisely for the people who need a translator. Registration can require a Chinese phone number for some features.
**Use it if** you read some Chinese already, or you are staying long enough for the interface to stop being a problem. **Skip it if** you land unable to read the menus of the app itself.

Not a translator, and that is the point. Pleco is the dictionary serious Chinese learners have used for over a decade: look up a character by drawing it, by radical, by pinyin, or with its camera, and get readings, definitions, example sentences and stroke order.
It will not translate a paragraph for you and does not try. For single words and characters it is better than anything else on this list, entirely offline, and the base app is free.
**Use it if** you are studying the language. **Skip it if** you want a sentence in and a sentence out.

The best translation quality on this list for long-form European-language text, and close to irrelevant for this trip. It needs a live connection, has no meaningful offline mode on mobile, and its reachability from mainland China is inconsistent.
**Use it if** you are translating documents from a connection that works. **Skip it if** you are standing in front of a menu in Chongqing.

sections.h2: Tova Translate, including where it loses
p: We built Tova for one specific gap: reading signs, menus and labels in a script you cannot pronounce, in a country where the obvious app does not work. It scans 11 writing systems, prints pinyin, Jyutping, romaji or Hangul romanisation **above each character**, and falls back to on-device translation when the network is gone.

Where it loses: **Pleco is a better dictionary** and always will be — it is a decade of lexicography, not a scanner. **DeepL translates long documents better.** **Apple Translate is free, already installed and good enough** if pronunciation does not matter to you. And on Android, Tova comes from Google Play, which is blocked in mainland China, so install it before you go.
**Use it if** you want to read and say the thing in front of you. **Skip it if** you only need the gist and already have an app that gives you one.

Each app was installed on an iPhone, given its offline packs on home Wi-Fi, then used on a mainland Chinese mobile network and on hotel Wi-Fi in September 2026. We checked whether the app reached its servers, whether the offline mode did what it claimed in aeroplane mode, and what the camera produced on printed menus and street signage. What each kind of offline download actually covers is in [the offline translator guide](/translate/offline-translator-china/).

We have an obvious interest in one of these answers. The way to check us is the aeroplane-mode test from [our China no-VPN guide](/translate/china-no-vpn/): it takes five minutes, it costs nothing, and it does not require trusting a comparison written by a competitor.

faqs.q: Does Google Translate work in China?
faqs.a: No, not over the network. Google's services are filtered in mainland China and the China-specific translate.google.cn was shut down in 2022. Offline language packs downloaded before you arrive do keep working, because they run on your phone rather than on Google's servers.

faqs.q: What is the best free translator app for China?
faqs.a: Apple Translate, if you carry an iPhone. It is not blocked, it is already installed, and it translates offline once you download Chinese in Settings. It will not show pronunciation above each character.

faqs.q: Do I need a VPN to translate in China?
faqs.a: Not if your app translates on the device. A VPN is only needed for apps that must reach blocked servers, and a VPN has to be installed and configured before you arrive — installing one from inside China is itself usually blocked.

faqs.q: Is Pleco better than Google Translate?
faqs.a: For looking up a single character or word, yes, and it works entirely offline. For translating a whole sentence or paragraph, no — Pleco is a dictionary rather than a translator, and does not try to be one.

faqs.q: Will a travel eSIM get around the block?
faqs.a: Often, but not always. Many roaming and travel eSIM plans route your data back through the home carrier's network, so blocked services load normally. Some route locally instead and are filtered like any Chinese connection. Check with the provider and do not make it your only plan.

title: Chinese Train Stations — Which One Is On Your Ticket
metaDesc: Hangzhou, Hangzhou East and Hangzhou South are three stations, one character apart. How to read 东 南 西 北 on a ticket, and why your passport is part of it.
keywords: chinese train station names, hangzhou east station, beijing west vs beijing south, shanghai hongqiao station, which train station china, china high speed rail passport
h1: Which Chinese train station is on your ticket?
lede: Most Chinese cities have three or four main stations and the English names differ by one word. Get it wrong and you are across town from a train you cannot rebook. The whole distinction is four characters.
steps: Find the station characters on your ticket or booking — they are next to the city name.
Check the last character before 站: 东 is East, 南 South, 西 West, 北 North.
Put that station into your map app in Chinese, not English, and check the travel time from where you are staying.

sections.h2: The mistake is one character wide
p: 杭州站, 杭州东站 and 杭州南站 are three separate stations in Hangzhou, several kilometres apart. In English they come out as Hangzhou, Hangzhou East and Hangzhou South — close enough that a tired traveller books one and turns up at another.

Chinese station names are built the same way every time: **city + direction + 站**. 站 (zhàn) means station. The character in front of it is the whole difference, and there are only four of them worth memorising.

This matters more than it sounds, because the fast trains usually do not leave from the station named plainly after the city. The plain one is often the old central station handling slower services; the high-speed lines were built later, on the edge of town, and got a direction in the name.

sections.callout: **上海虹桥 (Shanghai Hongqiao) shares its name with the airport**, and the station and terminal sit next to each other on the same metro stop. That is convenient if you are connecting and confusing if you are not — check whether your ticket says 虹桥站 or 虹桥机场.

sections.h2: Wuhan, where the stations do not say Wuhan
p: Every rule above assumes the station name contains the city name. Wuhan breaks it. Its three main stations are 武汉站, 汉口站 and 武昌站 — and two of those do not contain 武汉 at all.

Hankou (汉口) and Wuchang (武昌) are old districts of the city that kept their own names, so an English itinerary reading "Hankou" gives no clue that you are in Wuhan. Travellers have stood in the wrong one.
Other cities do this on a smaller scale. If a station name looks nothing like the city you booked, that is normal — look it up rather than assuming the booking is wrong.

sections.h2: Your passport is part of the ticket
p: Chinese rail runs on a real-name system, 实名制 (shímíngzhì). The ticket is tied to the passport used to buy it, and the passport has to be with you: you show it to enter the station, again at the gate, and it can be checked on board.

Practically that means the passport number goes in at booking, the name must match the passport exactly, and whoever travels has to be the person on the ticket. You cannot hand a spare ticket to a friend.

Foreign passports usually cannot use the automatic gates that residents tap through with an ID card. Look for the staffed lane at the end of the gate line — it is normal, it is quick, and it is the one that catches people who queued in the wrong place.

sections.h2: Reading the station on the day
p: Signage inside is consistent nationwide, so the same handful of characters gets you from the door to the platform.

head: Sign
Pinyin
What it is
rows: Waiting hall — where you sit until boarding
Ticket gate — the number here matches your ticket

ol: **Read the station in Chinese, not English.** The Chinese name is unambiguous; the English one is a transliteration that loses the direction if you skim.
**Search your map app with the Chinese characters.** Typing "Hangzhou station" can return any of three. Pasting 杭州东站 returns exactly one.
**Check the travel time from your hotel.** These stations are often 40 minutes apart, and the fast one is usually the far one.
**Confirm the passport name matches.** A middle name that is on the passport but not on the booking is a real problem at the gate, not a formality.
**Photograph the ticket.** You will want the 车次 train number and the 检票口 gate number when the departure board is a wall of characters and you have four minutes.

p: A translation app that gives you "Hangzhou East Railway Station" has technically answered, and you still cannot match it against the departure board, because the board says 杭州东站 and you are scanning for letters.

What helps is seeing the characters with the reading above them, so 东 stops being a shape and becomes dōng, East — something you can recognise at a glance on a ticket, a board, and a platform sign. Four characters is a very small thing to learn for how much it prevents.

faqs.q: What is the difference between Hangzhou and Hangzhou East station?
faqs.a: They are two different stations several kilometres apart. 杭州站 is the older central station; 杭州东站 (East) is the larger high-speed hub and is where most fast trains to Shanghai and Beijing leave from. Check which one your ticket names before you set off.

faqs.q: Which Shanghai station do high-speed trains use?
faqs.a: 上海虹桥站, Shanghai Hongqiao, handles most high-speed services. It sits beside Hongqiao Airport on the same metro stop, so confirm whether your ticket says the station (虹桥站) or the airport (虹桥机场).

faqs.q: Do I need my passport to take a train in China?
faqs.a: Yes. Chinese rail uses a real-name system: the ticket is tied to the passport it was booked with, and you show that passport to enter the station and again at the gate. The name on the booking has to match the passport exactly.

faqs.q: Why is the station called Hankou and not Wuhan?
faqs.a: Hankou (汉口) is a district of Wuhan that kept its own name, as did Wuchang (武昌). Wuhan has three main stations and only one of them, 武汉站, contains the city name. It is normal, not a booking error.

faqs.q: How do I tell which station a Chinese sign means?
faqs.a: Read the character immediately before 站: 东 is East, 南 South, 西 West, 北 North. A name with no direction character is usually the older central station. Scanning a sign or ticket with Tova prints the reading above each character so the direction is readable at a glance.
